title: Celsus parades the mysteries of Mithras
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις βουλόμενος ὁ Κέλσος πολυμάθειαν ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιδείξασθαι ἐν τῷ καθ᾿ ἡμῶν λόγῳ ἐκτίθεταί τινα καὶ Περσικὰ μυστήρια ἐν οἷς φησιν· αἰνίττεται ταῦτα καὶ ὁ Περσῶν λόγος, καὶ ἡ τοῦ Μίθρου τελετὴ, (ἣ) παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἐστιν. ἔστι γάρ τι ἐν αὐτῇ σύμβολον τῶν δύο τῶν ἐν οὐρανῷ περιόδων, τῆς τε ἀπλανοῦς καὶ τῆς εἰς τοὺς πλανήτας αὖ νενεμημένης, καὶ τῆς δι᾿ αὐτῶν τῆς ψυχῆς διεξόδου. τοιόνδε τὸ σύμβολον· κλῖμαξ ἑπτάπυλος, ἐπὶ δ᾿ αὐτῇ πύλη ὀγδόη. ἡ πρώτη τῶν πυλῶν μολίβδου, ἡ δευτέρα κασσιτέρου, ἡ τρίτη χαλκοῦ, ἡ τετάρτη σιδήρου, ἡ πέμπτη κεραστοῦ νομίσματος, ἡ ἕκτη ἀργύρου, χρυσοῦ δὲ ἡ ἑβδόμη. τὴν πρώτην τίθενται Κρόνου, τῷ μολίβδῳ τεκμηριούμενοι τὴν βραδυτῆτα τοῦ ἀστέρος, τὴν δευτέραν Ἀφροδίτης, παραβάλλοντες αὐτῇ τὸ φαιδρόν τε καὶ μαλακὸν τοῦ κασσιτέρου, τὴν τρίτην τοὺ Διὸς, τὴν χαλκοβατῆ καὶ στεῤῥὰν, τὴν τετάρτην Ἑρμοῦ, τλήμονα γὰρ ἔργων ἁπάντων καὶ χρηματιστὴν καὶ πολύκμητον εἶναι τόν τε σίδηρον καὶ τὸν Ἑρμῆν, τὴν πέμπτην Ἄρεος, τὴν ἐκ τοῦ κράματος ἀνώμαλόν τε καὶ ποικίλην, ἕκτην Σελήνης τὴν ἀργυρᾶν, ἑβδόμην Ἡλίου τὴν χρυσῆν, μιμούμενοι τὰς χρόας αὐτῶν. ἑξῆς ἐξετάζει τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς οὕτω κατειλεγμένης τάξεως τῶν ἀστέρων, δηλουμένης διὰ συμβόλων ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασι τῆς λοιπῆς ὕλης, καὶ μουσικοὺς λόγους προσάπτει ᾗ ἐκτίθεται Περσῶν θεολογίᾳ· προσφιλοτιμεῖται δὲ τούτοις καὶ δευτέραν ἐκθέσθαι διήγησιν, πάλιν ἐχομένην μουσικῶν θεωρημάτων. ἔδοξε δέ μοι τὸ ἐκθέσθαι τὴν λέξιν ἐν τούτοις τοῦ Κέλσου ἄτοπον εἶναι καὶ ὅμοιον ᾧ αὐτὸς πεποίηκεν, εἰς τὴν περὶ Χριστιανῶν καὶ Ἰουδαίων κατηγορίαν ἀκαίρως παραλαβὼν οὐ μόνον τὰ Πλάτωνος, ὡς ἐκείνοις ἀρκεῖσθαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ, ὥς φησι, Περσῶν τοῦ Μίθρου μυστήρια καὶ τὴν διήγησιν αὐτῶν. ὅπως ποτὲ γὰρ ἐχέτω ταῦτα, εἴτε ψευδῶς εἴτ᾿ ἀληθῶς, τοῖς τὰ τοῦ Μίθρου πρεσβεύουσι καὶ Πέρσαις· τί δὴ οὖν μᾶλλον ταῦτ᾿ ἐξέθετο ἤ τι τῶν λοιπῶν μυστηρίων μετὰ τῆς διηγήσεως αὐτῶν; οὐ γὰρ δοκεῖ παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν εἶναι ἐξαίρετα τὰ τοῦ Μίθρου παρὰ τὰ Ἐλευσίνια ἢ τὰ παραδιδόμενα τοῖς ἐν Αἰγίνῃ μυουμένοις τὰ τῆς Ἑκάτης. τί δὲ μᾶλλον εἴπερ βαρβαρικὰ ἐβούλετο μυστήρια ἐκτίθεσθαι μετὰ τῆς διηγήσεως αὐτῶν, οὐ μᾶλλον τὰ Αἰγυπτίων, ἐν οἷς πολλοὶ σεμνύνονται, ἢ τὰ Καππαδοκῶν περὶ τῆς ἐν Κομάνοις Ἀρτέμιδος ἢ τὰ Θρᾳκῶν ἢ καὶ τὰ Ῥωμαίων αὐτῶν, τελούντων τοὺς εὐγενεστάτους τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς συγκλήτου βουλῆς; ἀλλ᾿ εἰ ἄκαιρον αὐτῷ ἔδοξεν ἐκείνων τι παραβαλεῖν ὡς μηδαμῶς συμβαλλόμενον εἰς τὴν Ἰουδαίων ἢ Χριστιανῶν κατηγορίαν, πῶς οὐχὶ τὸ αὐτὸ ἄκαιρον καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκθέσεως τῶν Μιθραϊκῶν αὐτῷ ἐφαίνετο;
pass_a_gloss: Next after these Celsus, wishing to display (ἐπιδείκνυμι) his much-learning (πολυμάθεια) in the treatise (λόγος) against us, sets out also certain Persian mysteries (Περσικὰ μυστήρια), in which he says: 'These things also the teaching (λόγος) of the Persians hints (αἰνίττομαι) and the rite (τελετή) of Mithras which is among them. For there is in it a symbol (σύμβολον) of the two revolutions (περίοδοι) in heaven, of the fixed (ἀπλανής) and of that distributed (νέμω) in turn to the planets, and of the passage (διέξοδος) of the soul through them. Such is the symbol: a seven-gated (ἑπτάπυλος) ladder, and upon it an eighth gate (πύλη). The first of the gates of lead (μόλιβδος), the second of tin (κασσίτερος), the third of bronze (χαλκός), the fourth of iron (σίδηρος), the fifth of mixed coinage (κεραστὸν νόμισμα), the sixth of silver (ἄργυρος), and the seventh of gold (χρυσός). The first they set as Kronos's, by the lead inferring (τεκμηριόω) the slowness (βραδυτής) of the star (ἀστήρ); the second Aphrodite's, comparing (παραβάλλω) to her the bright (φαιδρόν) and soft (μαλακόν) of tin; the third Zeus's, the bronze-floored (χαλκοβατής) and firm (στερρά); the fourth Hermes's, for enduring (τλήμων) of all works and money-maker (χρηματιστής) and much-wrought/much-toiling (πολύκμητος) are both iron and Hermes; the fifth Ares's, the one from the mixture (κρᾶμα), uneven (ἀνώμαλος) and varied (ποικίλη); sixth the Moon's (Σελήνη), the silver; seventh the Sun's (Ἥλιος), the golden, imitating (μιμέομαι) their colours (χρόαι).' Next he examines (ἐξετάζω) the cause (αἰτία) of the order (τάξις) of the stars so listed (καταλέγω), shown through symbols in the names of the remaining matter (λοιπὴ ὕλη), and attaches (προσάπτω) musical ratios (μουσικοὶ λόγοι) to the Persian theology (θεολογία) he sets out; and he is ambitious besides (προσφιλοτιμέομαι) to set out also a second account (διήγησις), again holding to musical theorems (θεωρήματα). It seemed to me that setting out the saying (λέξις) of Celsus in these was absurd (ἄτοπον) and like what he himself has done, taking in (παραλαμβάνω) unseasonably (ἀκαίρως) into the accusation (κατηγορία) about Christians and Jews not only the things of Plato, so as to be content (ἀρκέομαι) with those, but also the, as he says, mysteries of Mithras of the Persians and their account. For however these things may stand, whether falsely or truly, for those honouring (πρεσβεύω) the things of Mithras and the Persians; why then did he set out these rather than one of the other mysteries with their account? For the things of Mithras do not seem among the Greeks to be exceptional (ἐξαίρετα) beside the Eleusinian or those handed down (παραδίδωμι) to those initiated (μυέω) in Aegina, the things of Hecate. And why rather, if he wished to set out barbarian (βαρβαρικά) mysteries with their account, not rather those of the Egyptians, in which many take pride (σεμνύνομαι), or those of the Cappadocians about the Artemis in Comana, or those of the Thracians, or even of the Romans themselves, initiating (τελέω) the most noble (εὐγενέστατοι) of those from the senate (σύγκλητος βουλή)? But if it seemed unseasonable (ἄκαιρον) to him to compare any of those as in no way contributing (συμβάλλομαι) to the accusation of Jews or Christians, how did not the same appear unseasonable to him also in the setting out (ἔκθεσις) of the Mithraic things?
pass_b_english: After this, Celsus, wishing to display his wide learning in his treatise against us, also sets out certain Persian mysteries, where he says: “These things are hinted at also by the teaching of the Persians and by the rite of Mithras that is among them. For in it there is a symbol of the two revolutions in heaven, that of the fixed stars and that assigned in turn to the planets, and of the soul’s passage through them. The symbol is this: a ladder with seven gates, and on top of it an eighth gate. The first of the gates is of lead, the second of tin, the third of bronze, the fourth of iron, the fifth of alloyed coin-metal, the sixth of silver, and the seventh of gold. The first they assign to Kronos, taking the lead as a sign of the slowness of that star; the second to Aphrodite, likening to her the brightness and softness of tin; the third to Zeus, the bronze-floored and solid one; the fourth to Hermes, for iron and Hermes alike endure every kind of work, make money, and toil hard; the fifth to Ares, the gate of mixed metal, uneven and varied; the sixth, the silver one, to the Moon; the seventh, the golden one, to the Sun, imitating their colours.”

Next he examines the reason for the stars being listed in this order, which is shown by symbols in the names of the rest of the materials, and he attaches musical ratios to the Persian theology he sets out. Not content with this, he takes pains to set out a second explanation as well, again bound up with musical theory.

But it seemed to me absurd to set out Celsus’s words on these matters. It would be like what he himself has done: in his accusation against Christians and Jews he brought in, out of season, not only the teachings of Plato, when he might have been content with those, but also what he calls the Persian mysteries of Mithras and their explanation. For however these things stand for those who honour the rites of Mithras and for the Persians, whether falsely or truly, why did he set out these rather than one of the other mysteries along with its explanation? For among the Greeks the mysteries of Mithras are not thought to be anything special compared with the Eleusinian mysteries, or with the rites of Hecate handed down to those initiated in Aegina.

And if he wanted to set out barbarian mysteries with their explanation, why not rather those of the Egyptians, in which many take pride, or those of the Cappadocians about the Artemis at Comana, or those of the Thracians, or even those of the Romans themselves, who initiate the noblest members of the Senate? But if he thought it out of place to bring in any of those, as contributing nothing to his accusation of Jews or Christians, how did the same thing not seem out of place to him when he set out the Mithraic rites?

choices.choice: Celsus’s direct quotation runs from αἰνίττεται ταῦτα to μιμούμενοι τὰς χρόας αὐτῶν; what follows (ἑξῆς ἐξετάζει …) is Origen’s summary. The relative ἥ before παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς is an editorial supplement (in angle/round brackets in the TEI), accepted. ‘These things’ at the start of the quotation = the soul’s road through the planets (6.21). κεραστοῦ νομίσματος: ‘alloyed coin-metal’ (coinage of mixed metal); the fifth gate is then called ‘the one from the mixture’ (ἐκ τοῦ κράματος). χαλκοβατῆ (‘with the bronze threshold/floor’) is a Homeric epithet of the house of Zeus (Iliad 1.426, Διὸς ποτὶ χαλκοβατὲς δῶ); πολύκμητος is Homer’s epithet for iron (‘much-wrought’, e.g. Iliad 6.48); rendered ‘much-toiling’ here because Celsus applies it to Hermes as well as iron; echoes noted only, not cited inline. Kronos = Saturn, Ares = Mars, Hermes = Mercury, Aphrodite = Venus, Zeus = Jupiter. ‘The names of the rest of the materials’ (ἐν τοῖς ὀνόμασι τῆς λοιπῆς ὕλης) is obscure; it may refer to the metals and colours beyond those already explained; kept literal. μουσικοὺς λόγους rendered ‘musical ratios’ (the Pythagorean ratios linking planets and notes). ‘Rites of Hecate … in Aegina’ and ‘Artemis at Comana’ (Comana in Cappadocia, cult of Ma identified with Artemis) are named by Origen; no further gloss in the text. ὅπως ποτὲ γὰρ ἐχέτω ταῦτα … is an imperative of concession (‘however these things stand’). No Scripture in this chapter.
τὴν χαλκοβατῆ καὶ στερράν: 'the gate with the bronze threshold, firm and solid' changed to 'the bronze-floored and solid one' (two Greek adjectives, not three)
τλήμονα ... χρηματιστὴν ... πολύκμητον: archaic 'patient of every kind of work, makers of money, and much-toiling' changed to 'endure every kind of work, make money, and toil hard'
μιμούμενοι τὰς χρόας αὐτῶν kept as a participle: 'imitating their colours' (was a new clause 'so they imitate')
restored the connective γάρ: 'For among the Greeks the mysteries of Mithras...'
checked: Celsus's direct quotation bounded αἰνίττεται ... χρόας αὐτῶν, Origen's summary after; no Scripture; no classical citation inline (Homeric epithets only noted)
